This document answers research question 1 of our project: *what drives the
real cost per square metre of new houses across New Zealand's districts?* It
starts from the model-ready table built by Niwesh (`rq1_model_data.csv`,
Step 1 of his pipeline), builds the modelling table we use for every model,
looks at the data before fitting anything, and then fits the models in the
order the course teaches them: simple and multiple linear regression (Modules
1–2), ridge and lasso (ISLR2 §6.5), a regression tree, a random forest and a
boosted model (Module 6). Every model is judged on the same time-ordered test
set (2020Q1–2026Q2) by test MSE and $R^2$, and the document ends with a
comparison against the numbers in Niwesh's own notebooks, so the group has
two independent builds of the same question.

# Set up

## Data

The table has one row per district and quarter. Niwesh's Step 1 notebook
(`01_rq1_data_preparation.Rmd`, branch `niwesh`) builds it from the Stats NZ
*Building consents by territorial authority (Monthly)* file: months are summed
to quarters, the consented value of new houses is divided by their floor area
to give nominal $/m², GST of the day is removed, the value is deflated to
June-2026 dollars with the CGPI dwelling-units index (`CEPQ.S611011A`) and 15%
GST is put back. Rows with fewer than five new houses in the quarter were
dropped before the file was written, so every row we read is a usable one.

```{r}
rq1_raw <- read_csv(file.path(data_root, "rq1_model_data.csv"),
                    show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(across(c(ta, region, island, split), as.factor),
         quarter = factor(quarter, levels = 1:4),
         is_city = as.logical(is_city),
         in_model = as.logical(in_model))

cat("Rows:", nrow(rq1_raw), " Columns:", ncol(rq1_raw),
    " Districts:", n_distinct(rq1_raw$ta),
    " Quarters:", min(rq1_raw$yq), "to", max(rq1_raw$yq), "\n")
glimpse(rq1_raw)
```

8,662 district-quarters, 67 districts, 1990Q2 to 2026Q2, 43 columns. The data
dictionary that travels with the file:

```{r}
read_csv(file.path(data_root, "rq1_data_dictionary.csv"),
         show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Data dictionary for rq1_model_data.csv (Niwesh, Step 1)")
```

## The modelling table

Not every column is a legitimate predictor. We keep two responses, the
drivers, and the two geography columns, and drop the rest. The rule for what
is a driver: it must be known in the same quarter from *counts* (how many of
what was consented) or from the past, never from the dollar value of the
houses themselves — otherwise the model is told the answer.

```{r}
# the two responses: relative cost (headline) and real $/m2 (secondary, section 6)
responses <- c("rel_log_cost_m2", "log_real_cost_m2")

# the drivers: same-quarter counts and shares, population pressure, and the time index
drivers <- c("t_index",             # quarter number, 1990Q1 = 1
             "avg_house_m2",        # average floor area of a new house
             "rel_house_m2",        # house size relative to the rest of NZ, same quarter
             "log_houses_n",        # log number of new houses
             "multiunit_share",     # share of new dwellings that are not stand-alone houses
             "apt_share",           # share that are apartments
             "retire_share",        # share that are retirement-village units
             "dwell_per_1000",      # new dwellings per 1,000 residents, year to quarter end
             "houses_yoy",          # log growth in houses vs the same quarter last year
             "log_resid_alt_real",  # log real $ of residential alterations
             "log_nonres_real")     # log real $ of new non-residential work

df <- rq1_raw %>%
  dplyr::select(ta, region, year, quarter, yq, split, houses_n,
                all_of(responses), all_of(drivers))

dim(df)
```

::: {.boxNote}
**What was left out, and why.** `nominal_cost_m2`, `houses_val`,
`real_cost_m2`, `loo_cost_m2` and `real_factor` are the response or its
ingredients (leakage). `real_cost_m2_lag1` / `_lag4` are the response one and
four quarters earlier — a persistence benchmark, not a driver of cost, so they
are kept out of the explanatory models. `houses_m2`, `dwell_n`, `apt_n`,
`retire_n`, `town_n`, `resid_new_val`, `resid_alt_val`, `nonres_new_val` are
the raw counts and dollars that the shares and logs above are built from, and
would duplicate them. `island`, `is_city` and `quarter` (season) explained
under 0.5% of the variance in Niwesh's EDA and are dropped as features;
`quarter` and `year` stay in the table for grouping only.

**Rows: our frame vs Niwesh's.** Niwesh fits his models on 1996Q1 onward and
drops Chatham Islands and Kawerau (5,694 train / 1,608 test, 65 districts). We
keep the full 1990Q2+ frame and all 67 districts as agreed on 6 Nov
(7,051 / 1,611). The practical difference is small — Chatham Islands has 2
rows and Kawerau 3 — but two drivers are not available before 1996:
`dwell_per_1000` (the per-1,000-residents series starts in 1996) is `NA` for
all 1,355 pre-1996 rows, and `houses_yoy` is `NA` for the first year of each
district (238 rows). Any model that uses them is therefore fitted on the rows
where they exist; the table below shows how many that is. Where we compare
against Niwesh's numbers in section 6 we say which frame each number comes
from.
:::

```{r}
# how many rows survive once the drivers that start in 1996 are required
df_complete <- df %>% drop_na(all_of(drivers))

bind_rows(
  df          %>% count(split, name = "all rows"),
  df_complete %>% count(split, name = "rows with every driver")
) %>%
  group_by(split) %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(.x, na.rm = TRUE))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Rows available per split")
```

## Train and test sets

The split is by time, not at random: the labs' `sample()` split would let
2024 rows teach the model about 2023, which is not the question a forecaster
faces. Niwesh's file carries the split already (`split == "train"` up to
2019Q4, `"test"` from 2020Q1), and we use it as given so both builds are
judged on exactly the same quarters.

```{r}
df_train <- df %>% dplyr::filter(split == "train")
df_test  <- df %>% dplyr::filter(split == "test")

cat("Training set size:", nrow(df_train), " (", min(df_train$yq), "to", max(df_train$yq), ")\n")
cat("Test set size:    ", nrow(df_test),  " (", min(df_test$yq),  "to", max(df_test$yq),  ")\n")
cat("Districts in train:", n_distinct(df_train$ta), " in test:", n_distinct(df_test$ta), "\n")
```

7,051 training and 1,611 test rows, all 67 districts in both. The test years
include COVID and the 2021–23 cost spike, so this is a hard test on purpose.

# First impression

Before fitting anything: what does the response look like, which districts
sit where, and how do the drivers relate to it and to each other.

## The two responses

```{r}
p1 <- ggplot(df_train, aes(x = log_real_cost_m2)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "Log real $/m2 (training rows)",
       x = "log(real $/m2, June-2026 dollars)", y = "District-quarters")

p2 <- ggplot(df_train, aes(x = rel_log_cost_m2)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "darkorange", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "Relative cost (training rows)",
       x = "log(district $/m2) - log(rest-of-NZ $/m2)", y = "District-quarters")

grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2)
```

Both are close to symmetric on the log scale, which is what the log was for.
The relative response is centred just below zero (the median district is
slightly cheaper than the country as a whole, because the national figure is
pulled up by Auckland) and most rows sit within ±0.3, i.e. within about 30%
of the rest of the country.

```{r}
df_train %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(real = median(exp(log_real_cost_m2)),
            relative = median(rel_log_cost_m2)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "response", values_to = "median") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = median)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ response, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1,
             labeller = as_labeller(c(real = "Median real $/m2 by year",
                                      relative = "Median relative cost by year"))) +
  labs(title = "Why the relative response exists", x = "Year", y = NULL)
```

The real $/m² series rises through the whole training period; the relative
series is flat by construction. A tree-based model cannot extrapolate a trend
past the last training year, and a linear trend in `t_index` would be asked to
hold through 2020–26 — the relative response removes the problem rather than
hoping a model copes with it. Section 6 fits the real response as well, to
show the size of the gap.

## Districts

```{r, out.width = '90%', fig.height = 7}
district_order <- df_train %>%
  group_by(ta) %>%
  summarise(med = median(rel_log_cost_m2)) %>%
  arrange(med) %>% pull(ta)

df_train %>%
  mutate(ta = factor(ta, levels = district_order)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = ta, y = rel_log_cost_m2, fill = region)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.4) +
  coord_flip() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Relative cost by district, 1990-2019",
       x = NULL, y = "log(district $/m2) - log(rest-of-NZ $/m2)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.text = element_text(size = 7),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6))
```

```{r}
df_train %>%
  group_by(ta, region) %>%
  summarise(median_ratio = exp(median(rel_log_cost_m2)),
            IQR = IQR(rel_log_cost_m2), rows = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(median_ratio)) %>%
  slice(c(1:6, (n() - 5):n())) %>%
  mutate(across(c(median_ratio, IQR), ~ round(.x, 2))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Six dearest and six cheapest districts (median ratio to the rest of NZ, training years)")
```

The ordering is stable enough to matter: the same districts stay at the top
and bottom for thirty years. That is the first clue that *where* explains a
lot, and it is why a district fixed effect is the ceiling we compare the
drivers against in section 3.

## How much is location, how much is time?

Three one-way fits with nothing but group means — the same idea as the labs'
"predict the average" baseline, applied to each grouping in turn.

$$R^2 = 1 - \frac{RSS}{TSS}, \qquad RSS = \Sigma_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \bar y_{g(i)})^2$$

```{r}
r2_group <- function(y, g) {
  tss <- sum((y - mean(y))^2)
  rss <- sum((y - ave(y, g, FUN = mean))^2)
  1 - rss / tss
}

tibble(grouping = c("District", "Region", "Year", "Quarter (season)", "District + year"),
       `relative cost` = c(r2_group(df_train$rel_log_cost_m2, df_train$ta),
                           r2_group(df_train$rel_log_cost_m2, df_train$region),
                           r2_group(df_train$rel_log_cost_m2, df_train$year),
                           r2_group(df_train$rel_log_cost_m2, df_train$quarter),
                           r2_group(df_train$rel_log_cost_m2, interaction(df_train$ta, df_train$year))),
       `log real $/m2` = c(r2_group(df_train$log_real_cost_m2, df_train$ta),
                           r2_group(df_train$log_real_cost_m2, df_train$region),
                           r2_group(df_train$log_real_cost_m2, df_train$year),
                           r2_group(df_train$log_real_cost_m2, df_train$quarter),
                           r2_group(df_train$log_real_cost_m2, interaction(df_train$ta, df_train$year)))) %>%
  mutate(across(-grouping, ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Share of training variance explained by group means alone")
```

On the relative response the district alone explains about a third of the
variance and the year almost none — time has been taken out. On the real
response it is the other way round: the year explains about 40% and the
district under 20%. Season explains nothing on either, which is why `quarter`
is not a feature. Whatever the drivers achieve in the next sections has to be
read against the district-only number: a model of measured drivers that
reaches it has explained *why* the dear districts are dear.

## The drivers

```{r, out.width = '100%', fig.height = 9}
set.seed(462)
df_train %>%
  drop_na(all_of(drivers)) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 1500) %>%
  dplyr::select(rel_log_cost_m2, all_of(drivers)) %>%
  ggpairs(lower = list(continuous = wrap("points", alpha = 0.2, size = 0.4)),
          upper = list(continuous = wrap("cor", size = 2.5)),
          progress = FALSE) +
  theme_grey(base_size = 6)
```

```{r}
cor_long <- df_train %>%
  drop_na(all_of(drivers)) %>%
  dplyr::select(all_of(drivers)) %>%
  cor() %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("x") %>%
  pivot_longer(-x, names_to = "y", values_to = "r")

ggplot(cor_long, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r)), size = 2.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "darkorange", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Correlation between the drivers (training rows with every driver)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

# the pairs that will matter for ridge vs lasso
cor_long %>%
  dplyr::filter(x < y, abs(r) > 0.6) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(r))) %>%
  mutate(r = round(r, 2)) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Driver pairs with |r| > 0.6")
```

Two pairs are strongly related: `avg_house_m2` with `rel_house_m2`
($r \approx 0.9$; the second is the first measured against the rest of the
country, so they move together within a quarter) and `log_houses_n` with
`log_resid_alt_real` ($r \approx 0.8$; big districts build more and renovate
more). `log_nonres_real` sits at about 0.7 with both of the size measures for
the same reason. Ordinary least squares will split the credit
between the members of each pair arbitrarily and give wide standard errors;
this is exactly the situation ridge and lasso are for, and section 4 shows
them handling it differently.

```{r}
df_train %>%
  group_by(ta) %>%
  summarise(across(c(rel_log_cost_m2, log_resid_alt_real, dwell_per_1000, avg_house_m2),
                   ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE))) %>%
  pivot_longer(-c(ta, rel_log_cost_m2), names_to = "driver", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = rel_log_cost_m2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "darkorange") +
  facet_wrap(~ driver, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "District averages, 1990-2019: three drivers against relative cost",
       x = "District mean of the driver", y = "District mean relative cost")
```

At the district level the picture is already readable: districts with more
alteration spending and bigger houses are dearer per m²; the population
pressure measure is positive but noisier. These are between-district
relationships. The models in the next sections are fitted on district-quarters,
so they also see how a district's cost moves when its own alterations or
growth change from one quarter to the next.

*Which model does best with these drivers — and does any of them reach the
district-only ceiling?*

# Linear regression

## The rows every model is fitted on

Two drivers do not exist for the early years: `dwell_per_1000` starts in 1996
and `houses_yoy` needs the same quarter a year earlier. `lm()` would drop the
affected rows silently and `glmnet()` refuses missing values altogether, so we
do it once, in the open, and every model from here on is fitted and tested on
the same rows.

```{r}
df_train_c <- df_train %>% drop_na(all_of(drivers))
df_test_c  <- df_test  %>% drop_na(all_of(drivers))

cat("Training rows with every driver:", nrow(df_train_c),
    " (", min(df_train_c$yq), "to", max(df_train_c$yq), ")\n")
cat("Test rows with every driver:    ", nrow(df_test_c),
    " (", min(df_test_c$yq),  "to", max(df_test_c$yq),  ")\n")

# the drivers-only frames the models see (no identifiers, one response)
train_drv <- df_train_c %>% dplyr::select(rel_log_cost_m2, all_of(drivers))
test_drv  <- df_test_c  %>% dplyr::select(rel_log_cost_m2, all_of(drivers))
```

::: {.boxNote}
**Headline frame: 5,696 training and 1,611 test district-quarters.** That is
every row from 1996Q1 onward, all 67 districts (the `houses_yoy` gaps are all
in 1990–91, inside the rows the 1996 cut already removes). It is Niwesh's modelling frame plus
one Chatham Islands row and one Kawerau row, so the two builds are directly
comparable. The cost of keeping the two drivers is the 1,355 rows from
1990–1995; section 6 fits the headline linear model without those two drivers
on all 7,051 rows as a sensitivity check, so the reader can see what the early
years would have added.
:::

Two helpers used throughout: the test-set metrics the labs compute by hand,
wrapped so every model reports them the same way, and a running results table.

$$MSE = \frac{1}{n}\Sigma_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat y_i)^2, \qquad
  R^2_{test} = 1 - \frac{\Sigma(y_i - \hat y_i)^2}{\Sigma(y_i - \bar y_{train})^2}$$

```{r}
y_train_mean <- mean(train_drv$rel_log_cost_m2)

test_metrics <- function(pred, actual) {
  mse <- mean((actual - pred)^2)
  c(test_MSE  = mse,
    test_RMSE = sqrt(mse),
    test_R2   = 1 - sum((actual - pred)^2) / sum((actual - y_train_mean)^2))
}

results <- tibble(model = character(), set = character(),
                  train_R2 = numeric(), adj_R2 = numeric(),
                  test_MSE = numeric(), test_RMSE = numeric(), test_R2 = numeric())

add_result <- function(results, model, set, fit_R2 = NA, fit_adjR2 = NA, metrics) {
  results %>% add_row(model = model, set = set,
                      train_R2 = fit_R2, adj_R2 = fit_adjR2,
                      test_MSE = metrics[["test_MSE"]],
                      test_RMSE = metrics[["test_RMSE"]],
                      test_R2 = metrics[["test_R2"]])
}
```

## Simple linear regression, by hand and by `lm()`

The single strongest driver at district level was residential alteration
spending (section 2). One predictor, the Module 1 formulas, then `lm()` to
confirm them.

$$b_1 = \frac{\Sigma_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)}{\Sigma_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar x)^2},
  \qquad b_0 = \bar y - b_1 \bar x$$

```{r}
x <- train_drv$log_resid_alt_real
y <- train_drv$rel_log_cost_m2

# slope and intercept from the formulas
b1 <- sum((x - mean(x)) * (y - mean(y))) / sum((x - mean(x))^2)
b0 <- mean(y) - b1 * mean(x)

# the same model with lm()
slr.fit <- lm(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ log_resid_alt_real, data = train_drv)

cat(sprintf("By hand: b0 = %.4f, b1 = %.4f\n", b0, b1))
cat(sprintf("lm():    b0 = %.4f, b1 = %.4f\n", coef(slr.fit)[1], coef(slr.fit)[2]))
```

```{r}
summary(slr.fit)

# confidence interval for b1 from the t distribution, then confint() to check
n     <- nrow(train_drv)
se_b1 <- summary(slr.fit)$coefficients["log_resid_alt_real", "Std. Error"]
t_crit <- qt(1 - 0.05 / 2, df = n - 2)
cat(sprintf("95%% CI for b1 by hand: (%.4f, %.4f)\n", b1 - t_crit * se_b1, b1 + t_crit * se_b1))
confint(slr.fit)
```

```{r}
ggplot(train_drv, aes(x = log_resid_alt_real, y = rel_log_cost_m2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1, size = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(intercept = b0, slope = b1, colour = "darkorange", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Simple linear regression: relative cost on log alteration spending",
       x = "log(real $ of residential alterations in the quarter)",
       y = "Relative cost")
```

```{r}
pred_slr <- predict(slr.fit, newdata = test_drv)
m_slr    <- test_metrics(pred_slr, test_drv$rel_log_cost_m2)
results  <- add_result(results, "Simple linear regression", "one driver",
                       summary(slr.fit)$r.squared, summary(slr.fit)$adj.r.squared, m_slr)
paste("The test MSE of the SLR model is", round(m_slr[["test_MSE"]], 5))
```

The slope is positive and many standard errors from zero: a district that
spends more on alterations in a quarter is dearer per m² for new houses in
that quarter. On its own, though, one driver explains about 12% of the
variation ($R^2 = 0.12$), and the cloud around the line is wide. Alteration
spending is a proxy for a busy, wealthy market, not the cost itself.

## Multiple linear regression on the drivers

All eleven drivers at once.

```{r}
mlr.fit <- lm(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = train_drv)
summary(mlr.fit)
```

The raw coefficients are not comparable (a one-unit change in `t_index` is a
quarter; in `multiunit_share` it is the whole range), so we also show each
coefficient multiplied by its predictor's standard deviation: the change in
relative cost for a one-SD change in the driver.

```{r}
std_coef <- function(fit, data) {
  b  <- coef(fit)[-1]
  b  <- b[names(b) %in% names(data)]          # numeric drivers only (skips factor dummies)
  sds <- sapply(names(b), function(v) sd(data[[v]]))
  tibble(driver = names(b), coefficient = b, std_coefficient = b * sds)
}

std_coef(mlr.fit, train_drv) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(std_coefficient))) %>%
  mutate(across(-driver, ~ round(.x, 4))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "MLR coefficients, raw and per one SD of the driver (training rows)")
```

```{r, fig.height = 7, out.width = '90%'}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(mlr.fit)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The diagnostic plots the labs list but never run. Residuals against fitted
values show no curve and roughly constant spread; the Q-Q plot has heavier
tails than a normal — a handful of very dear or very cheap district-quarters
— but nothing that bends the line; no point approaches a Cook's distance that
would change the fit if removed. The linear model is a fair description, with
the caveat that the extremes are under-predicted in both directions.

```{r}
pred_mlr <- predict(mlr.fit, newdata = test_drv)
m_mlr    <- test_metrics(pred_mlr, test_drv$rel_log_cost_m2)
results  <- add_result(results, "Multiple linear regression", "drivers",
                       summary(mlr.fit)$r.squared, summary(mlr.fit)$adj.r.squared, m_mlr)
paste("The test MSE of the MLR model is", round(m_mlr[["test_MSE"]], 5))
```

Read the coefficient table with the correlation heatmap in mind: `avg_house_m2`
and `rel_house_m2` carry opposite signs, and so do `log_houses_n` and
`log_resid_alt_real`. That is the signature of collinearity — least squares has
split the shared signal between the two members of each pair, and the
individual coefficients should not be read as effect sizes. Section 4 is the
remedy.

## Adding the district

`ta` as a 67-level factor is the fixed-effects ceiling from section 2: it
absorbs everything about a district that does not change over time. If the
drivers were a full explanation of why dear districts are dear, adding `ta`
would add nothing. `lm()` can hold a factor this size; the tree-based models
in section 5 cannot, which is why they get `region` instead.

```{r}
train_ta <- df_train_c %>% dplyr::select(rel_log_cost_m2, all_of(drivers), ta)
test_ta  <- df_test_c  %>% dplyr::select(rel_log_cost_m2, all_of(drivers), ta)

mlr_ta.fit <- lm(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = train_ta)

cat("Adjusted R2, drivers only:    ", round(summary(mlr.fit)$adj.r.squared, 3), "\n")
cat("Adjusted R2, drivers + district:", round(summary(mlr_ta.fit)$adj.r.squared, 3), "\n")

# the drivers' coefficients once district is held fixed (within-district effects)
std_coef(mlr_ta.fit, train_ta) %>%
  dplyr::filter(driver %in% drivers) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(std_coefficient))) %>%
  mutate(across(-driver, ~ round(.x, 4))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Driver coefficients with district fixed effects (within-district)")
```

```{r}
pred_mlr_ta <- predict(mlr_ta.fit, newdata = test_ta)
m_mlr_ta    <- test_metrics(pred_mlr_ta, test_ta$rel_log_cost_m2)
results     <- add_result(results, "Multiple linear regression", "drivers + district",
                          summary(mlr_ta.fit)$r.squared, summary(mlr_ta.fit)$adj.r.squared, m_mlr_ta)
paste("The test MSE of the MLR + district model is", round(m_mlr_ta[["test_MSE"]], 5))
```

The district dummies lift the fit well above the drivers alone, which answers
part of RQ1 on its own: the measured drivers explain some of the gap between
districts, but a large share is a location premium they do not capture. The
within-district coefficients are the more trustworthy reading of each driver,
because they compare a district with itself over time rather than Queenstown
with Ōpōtiki.

## Forward selection

Which drivers earn their place? Module 2's recipe: `regsubsets()` builds the
best model of each size by forward selection, and the size is chosen on data
the model did not see. Instead of a random validation set we hold out the last
four training years (2016–2019), because the test set is also "the future".

```{r}
# inner split: fit on 1996-2015, choose the size on 2016-2019
inner_fit   <- df_train_c %>% dplyr::filter(year <= 2015) %>% dplyr::select(rel_log_cost_m2, all_of(drivers))
inner_valid <- df_train_c %>% dplyr::filter(year >  2015) %>% dplyr::select(rel_log_cost_m2, all_of(drivers))

fwd.fit <- regsubsets(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = inner_fit,
                      nvmax = length(drivers), method = "forward")
fwd_summary <- summary(fwd.fit)

# validation MSE for each model size, the way Lab M2 does it
make_predictions <- function(object, newdata, size) {
  form  <- as.formula(object$call[[2]])
  mat   <- model.matrix(form, newdata)
  coefi <- coef(object, id = size)
  mat[, names(coefi)] %*% coefi
}

valid_mse <- sapply(1:length(drivers), function(size) {
  pred <- make_predictions(fwd.fit, inner_valid, size)
  mean((inner_valid$rel_log_cost_m2 - pred)^2)
})

best_size <- which.min(valid_mse)
tibble(size = 1:length(drivers), valid_MSE = valid_mse,
       adj_R2 = fwd_summary$adjr2, BIC = fwd_summary$bic) %>%
  mutate(across(-size, ~ round(.x, 5))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Forward selection: validation MSE (2016-2019), adjusted R2 and BIC by model size")
```

```{r}
plot(1:length(drivers), valid_mse, type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "Number of drivers", ylab = "Validation MSE (2016-2019)",
     main = "Forward selection: choosing the model size")
points(best_size, valid_mse[best_size], col = "darkorange", pch = 19, cex = 2)
```

```{r}
cat("Size with the lowest validation MSE:", best_size, "\n")
cat("Order in which forward selection added the drivers:\n")
print(apply(fwd_summary$which[, -1], 1, function(r) paste(names(r)[r], collapse = ", ")))

# refit the chosen size on all training rows and test it once
chosen <- names(coef(fwd.fit, id = best_size))[-1]
fwd_best.fit <- lm(reformulate(chosen, response = "rel_log_cost_m2"), data = train_drv)
pred_fwd <- predict(fwd_best.fit, newdata = test_drv)
m_fwd    <- test_metrics(pred_fwd, test_drv$rel_log_cost_m2)
results  <- add_result(results, paste0("Forward selection (", best_size, " drivers)"), "drivers",
                       summary(fwd_best.fit)$r.squared, summary(fwd_best.fit)$adj.r.squared, m_fwd)
paste("The test MSE of the forward-selected model is", round(m_fwd[["test_MSE"]], 5))
```

The order the drivers enter is the plain-language ranking of what matters
when each is allowed to add only what the earlier ones missed: alteration
spending first, population pressure second, the number of houses third. The
validation curve does not flatten — it bottoms at three drivers and then
rises, so on the 2016–2019 years every further driver made the predictions
slightly worse. Yet the three-driver model then tests *worse* than the full
eleven-driver MLR on 2020–2026 (0.01506 against 0.01459). The validation
years and the test years disagree about how complex the model should be,
which is a fair warning about choosing anything on four years of data; the
honest reading is that the three drivers carry most of the signal and the
other eight are worth a little in some periods and nothing in others. Keep
this in mind for section 4 — the lasso reaches the same three by a different
route.

## Two transformations worth a look

Module 2 adds terms inside the formula rather than new columns. Two are
suggested by section 2: population pressure may act with diminishing returns
(a squared term), and alteration spending may matter more in a district that
is also building a lot (an interaction).

```{r}
mlr_poly.fit <- lm(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ . - dwell_per_1000 + poly(dwell_per_1000, 2), data = train_drv)
mlr_int.fit  <- lm(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ . + log_resid_alt_real:log_houses_n, data = train_drv)

tibble(model = c("MLR, drivers", "+ poly(dwell_per_1000, 2)", "+ log_resid_alt_real:log_houses_n"),
       adj_R2 = c(summary(mlr.fit)$adj.r.squared,
                  summary(mlr_poly.fit)$adj.r.squared,
                  summary(mlr_int.fit)$adj.r.squared),
       test_MSE = c(m_mlr[["test_MSE"]],
                    test_metrics(predict(mlr_poly.fit, test_drv), test_drv$rel_log_cost_m2)[["test_MSE"]],
                    test_metrics(predict(mlr_int.fit,  test_drv), test_drv$rel_log_cost_m2)[["test_MSE"]])) %>%
  mutate(across(-model, ~ round(.x, 5))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Two transformations against the plain MLR")

# R names the term in formula order (log_houses_n:log_resid_alt_real), so find it by pattern
int_coef <- summary(mlr_int.fit)$coefficients
int_coef[grepl("log_houses_n.*log_resid_alt_real|log_resid_alt_real.*log_houses_n", rownames(int_coef)), , drop = FALSE]
```

Neither transformation is kept in the headline model unless it moves the test
MSE by more than the models in section 4 differ from each other — the reader
should judge that from the table. The interaction's sign is worth noting even
if small: a negative value says the alteration premium is weaker in districts
that are already building a lot, which is consistent with Niwesh's partial
dependence plot (his fig25).

*Eleven correlated drivers and a model that splits their credit arbitrarily —
can shrinkage give a steadier answer?*

# Ridge and lasso

Both fit the same linear model as section 3 but add a penalty on the size of
the coefficients. The tuning parameter $\lambda$ sets how hard the penalty
bites; $\lambda = 0$ is ordinary least squares.

$$\text{Ridge:}\quad \min_b \; \Sigma_{i=1}^{n}\Big(y_i - b_0 - \Sigma_{j=1}^{p} b_j x_{ij}\Big)^2 + \lambda \Sigma_{j=1}^{p} b_j^2$$

$$\text{Lasso:}\quad \min_b \; \Sigma_{i=1}^{n}\Big(y_i - b_0 - \Sigma_{j=1}^{p} b_j x_{ij}\Big)^2 + \lambda \Sigma_{j=1}^{p} |b_j|$$

The squared penalty shrinks every coefficient towards zero but never to zero;
the absolute penalty can set coefficients exactly to zero, so the lasso also
selects. With a correlated pair, ridge tends to share the effect between the
two; the lasso tends to keep one and drop the other. This is the ISLR2 §6.5
recipe with `glmnet`, the one package here that is not in a course lab.

## Set up

`glmnet()` wants a numeric matrix and standardises the columns itself
(`standardize = TRUE` is the default), so the penalty treats every driver
equally whatever its units.

```{r}
x_train <- model.matrix(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = train_drv)[, -1]   # drop the intercept column
y_train <- train_drv$rel_log_cost_m2
x_test  <- model.matrix(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = test_drv)[, -1]
y_test  <- test_drv$rel_log_cost_m2

dim(x_train)
```

## Choosing lambda with time-ordered folds

`cv.glmnet()` picks $\lambda$ by cross-validation. Its default folds are
random, which would again let later quarters inform earlier ones. We hand it
folds made of year blocks instead — five contiguous blocks of the training
years — so each fold is validated on years its training folds did not see.

```{r}
# five contiguous year blocks: 1996-2003, 2004-07, 2008-11, 2012-15, 2016-19
foldid <- cut(df_train_c$year, breaks = c(1995, 2003, 2007, 2011, 2015, 2019), labels = FALSE)
table(foldid)

cv.ridge <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 0, foldid = foldid)
cv.lasso <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 1, foldid = foldid)

cat(sprintf("Ridge: lambda.min = %.5f, lambda.1se = %.5f\n", cv.ridge$lambda.min, cv.ridge$lambda.1se))
cat(sprintf("Lasso: lambda.min = %.5f, lambda.1se = %.5f\n", cv.lasso$lambda.min, cv.lasso$lambda.1se))
```

```{r, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = '100%'}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(cv.ridge, main = "Ridge: CV error by lambda")
plot(cv.lasso, main = "Lasso: CV error by lambda")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Two values of $\lambda$ are marked on each curve: `lambda.min`, where the CV
error is lowest, and `lambda.1se`, the largest $\lambda$ whose error is within
one standard error of that minimum — the simplest model that is not
measurably worse. We report both. Note how far apart they are here (ridge
0.0037 against 0.138; lasso 0.00004 against 0.0145): with only five
time-block folds, and folds that differ from each other in how hard they are
to predict, the standard error of the CV curve is wide, and "within one SE" is
a generous margin. Section 4.5 shows what that costs on the test set. The
numbers on top of the lasso plot are how many drivers are still non-zero.

## Coefficient paths

```{r, fig.height = 5, out.width = '100%'}
ridge.fit <- glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 0)
lasso.fit <- glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 1)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(ridge.fit, xvar = "lambda", label = TRUE, main = "Ridge coefficient paths")
abline(v = log(cv.ridge$lambda.1se), lty = 2)
plot(lasso.fit, xvar = "lambda", label = TRUE, main = "Lasso coefficient paths")
abline(v = log(cv.lasso$lambda.1se), lty = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# which number is which driver on the plots
tibble(label = seq_along(colnames(x_train)), driver = colnames(x_train)) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Curve labels on the path plots")
```

Read the plots right to left (large $\lambda$ to small). Ridge's curves all
leave zero together and grow smoothly; the lasso's leave one at a time, and
the order they enter is a ranking of the drivers. The dashed line is
`lambda.1se`.

## Which drivers survive?

The table the poster needs: OLS, ridge and lasso side by side, standardised so
the sizes compare. A coefficient of 0 in the lasso columns means the driver
was dropped.

```{r}
x_sd <- apply(x_train, 2, sd)

coef_at <- function(cvfit, s) as.vector(coef(cvfit, s = s))[-1]   # drop the intercept

coef_table <- tibble(driver = colnames(x_train),
                     OLS = coef(mlr.fit)[colnames(x_train)],
                     `Ridge (1se)` = coef_at(cv.ridge, "lambda.1se"),
                     `Ridge (min)` = coef_at(cv.ridge, "lambda.min"),
                     `Lasso (1se)` = coef_at(cv.lasso, "lambda.1se"),
                     `Lasso (min)` = coef_at(cv.lasso, "lambda.min")) %>%
  mutate(across(-driver, ~ .x * x_sd))   # per one SD of the driver

coef_table %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(`Lasso (1se)`)), desc(abs(`Ridge (1se)`))) %>%
  mutate(across(-driver, ~ round(.x, 4))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Standardised coefficients (change in relative cost per one SD of the driver)")

cat("Drivers the lasso sets to zero at lambda.1se:",
    paste(coef_table$driver[coef_table$`Lasso (1se)` == 0], collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Drivers the lasso sets to zero at lambda.min:",
    paste(coef_table$driver[coef_table$`Lasso (min)` == 0], collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

```{r, fig.height = 5}
coef_table %>%
  dplyr::select(driver, OLS, `Ridge (1se)`, `Lasso (1se)`) %>%
  pivot_longer(-driver, names_to = "model", values_to = "std_coefficient") %>%
  mutate(driver = fct_reorder(driver, abs(std_coefficient), .fun = max)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = driver, y = std_coefficient, fill = model)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "What each model says about each driver",
       x = NULL, y = "Standardised coefficient", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Look first at the two correlated pairs from section 2. Under OLS
`log_houses_n` and `log_resid_alt_real` carry opposite signs (−0.030 and
+0.061 per SD); ridge at `lambda.1se` pulls them to the same sign (+0.005 and
+0.011) by sharing the credit; the lasso at `lambda.1se` keeps alteration
spending and sets the house count to zero. The house-size pair goes the same
way: OLS gives them opposite signs, ridge shrinks both to nearly nothing, the
lasso drops both. At `lambda.1se` the lasso keeps exactly two drivers —
`log_resid_alt_real` and `dwell_per_1000` — the first two that forward
selection chose; at `lambda.min` it keeps all eleven and its coefficients are
within 0.001 of OLS. So the two penalised models agree with each other
and with section 3.5 on what matters, and that agreement, not any single
coefficient, is the answer to "which parameters are important": alteration
spending and population pressure are the drivers of relative cost the data
will support in a linear model, with the number of houses a distant third.

## Test performance

```{r}
for (nm in c("lambda.1se", "lambda.min")) {
  m_r <- test_metrics(as.vector(predict(cv.ridge, newx = x_test, s = nm)), y_test)
  m_l <- test_metrics(as.vector(predict(cv.lasso, newx = x_test, s = nm)), y_test)
  results <- add_result(results, paste0("Ridge (", nm, ")"), "drivers", metrics = m_r)
  results <- add_result(results, paste0("Lasso (", nm, ")"), "drivers", metrics = m_l)
}

results %>%
  dplyr::filter(set == "drivers") %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 5))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Drivers-only models so far: training fit and test error")
```

At `lambda.min`, ridge and lasso test within a hair of OLS (0.01468 and
0.01458 against 0.01459): with eleven drivers and over five thousand rows the
model is not over-fitted, so there is nothing for the penalty to fix. At
`lambda.1se` both are clearly worse (0.01618 and 0.01669; test $R^2$ falls
from 0.21 to 0.13 and 0.10) — the one-SE rule, applied to a CV curve with
wide standard errors, threw away real signal. The lesson for this dataset is
to use `lambda.min` when the model has to predict, and to use the lasso's
*path* — the order in which drivers enter as $\lambda$ falls — when the
question is which drivers matter. The gain from shrinkage here is in reading
the coefficients, not in the error.

## Ridge and lasso with region

A penalised model cannot hold a 67-level district factor sensibly (each dummy
would be shrunk towards zero regardless of how well it is estimated), but the
17 region dummies are a fair middle ground between "drivers only" and "drivers
plus district".

```{r}
train_reg <- df_train_c %>% dplyr::select(rel_log_cost_m2, all_of(drivers), region)
test_reg  <- df_test_c  %>% dplyr::select(rel_log_cost_m2, all_of(drivers), region)

x_train_reg <- model.matrix(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = train_reg)[, -1]
x_test_reg  <- model.matrix(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = test_reg)[, -1]

cv.ridge.reg <- cv.glmnet(x_train_reg, y_train, alpha = 0, foldid = foldid)
cv.lasso.reg <- cv.glmnet(x_train_reg, y_train, alpha = 1, foldid = foldid)

for (nm in c("lambda.1se", "lambda.min")) {
  m_r <- test_metrics(as.vector(predict(cv.ridge.reg, newx = x_test_reg, s = nm)), y_test)
  m_l <- test_metrics(as.vector(predict(cv.lasso.reg, newx = x_test_reg, s = nm)), y_test)
  results <- add_result(results, paste0("Ridge (", nm, ")"), "drivers + region", metrics = m_r)
  results <- add_result(results, paste0("Lasso (", nm, ")"), "drivers + region", metrics = m_l)
}

# the region dummies the lasso keeps, and the driver coefficients once region is in
lasso_reg_coef <- as.vector(coef(cv.lasso.reg, s = "lambda.1se"))[-1]
names(lasso_reg_coef) <- colnames(x_train_reg)

cat("Region dummies kept by the lasso at lambda.1se:\n")
print(round(lasso_reg_coef[grepl("^region", names(lasso_reg_coef)) & lasso_reg_coef != 0], 4))

results %>%
  dplyr::filter(grepl("Ridge|Lasso", model)) %>%
  arrange(set, model) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 5))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Ridge and lasso: drivers only vs drivers + region")
```

The regions the lasso keeps are the ones whose premium or discount the
drivers cannot account for; the regions it drops are explained by their
drivers. Three survive at `lambda.1se`: Wellington (+0.025) and Hawke's Bay
(+0.014) dearer than their drivers say, Manawatū-Whanganui (−0.010) cheaper.
Auckland, Canterbury and Otago do not appear — their premiums are carried by
the drivers, Auckland's by population pressure and alteration spending in
particular. With region in, ridge and lasso at `lambda.min` test at 0.01357,
between the drivers-only MLR (0.01459) and the district model (0.01179): the
17 regions recover about a third of what the 67 districts know. That list is
a compact answer to the "location premium" half of RQ1 and sits naturally
beside the district ranking from section 2.

*The linear family has had its say. Do models that can find thresholds and
interactions on their own — trees — see anything the straight lines missed?*

# Tree-based models

Trees split the data on one driver at a time, so they find thresholds and
interactions without being told where to look, and they are indifferent to
the collinearity that troubled section 3. Their weakness is the opposite of
the linear model's: a tree can only predict values it has seen, so it cannot
follow a trend out of the training years. The models here are fitted on the
drivers plus `region` — `tree()` caps a factor at 32 levels and
`randomForest()` at 53, so the 67-level `ta` cannot go in. Module 6's recipe
throughout.

```{r}
# short region codes, so a split on several regions fits on the tree plot
region_short <- c("Northland Region" = "Nthld", "Auckland Region" = "Akl",
                  "Waikato Region" = "Wkto", "Bay of Plenty Region" = "BoP",
                  "Gisborne Region" = "Gis", "Hawke's Bay Region" = "HB",
                  "Taranaki Region" = "Tnki", "Manawatu-Whanganui Region" = "MWh",
                  "Wellington Region" = "Wgtn", "Tasman Region" = "Tas",
                  "Nelson Region" = "Nsn", "Marlborough Region" = "Marl",
                  "West Coast Region" = "WC", "Canterbury Region" = "Cant",
                  "Otago Region" = "Otago", "Southland Region" = "Sthld",
                  "Area Outside Region" = "Chat")

# data.frames rather than tibbles: gbm() in particular wants the base class
train_tree <- as.data.frame(train_reg) %>%
  mutate(region = factor(region_short[as.character(region)], levels = unname(region_short)))
test_tree  <- as.data.frame(test_reg) %>%
  mutate(region = factor(region_short[as.character(region)], levels = unname(region_short)))

stopifnot(!anyNA(train_tree$region), !anyNA(test_tree$region))

tibble(code = unname(region_short), region = names(region_short)) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Region codes used in the tree plots")
```

## Regression tree

```{r}
tree.fit <- tree(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = train_tree)
summary(tree.fit)
```

```{r, fig.width = 13, fig.height = 7, out.width = '100%'}
# type = "uniform" gives every level the same height; the default scales branch
# length by deviance, which leaves the first split with the whole canvas
plot(tree.fit, type = "uniform")
text(tree.fit, pretty = 0, cex = 0.7, digits = 3)
```

The first split is the plain-language headline of the tree: whichever driver
sits at the top is the single most useful yes/no question about a
district-quarter. The leaves are mean relative costs for the rows that reach
them. A split on `region` lists the codes that go left; everything else goes
right. Branch lengths carry no information in this layout; the node listing
below gives each split's rows, deviance and mean, which is where the worth of
a split is read.

```{r}
tree.fit
```

Module 6 prunes with cross-validation: grow the full tree, ask how the
deviance changes with the number of leaves, and cut back to the size with the
lowest CV deviance.

```{r}
set.seed(462)
cv.reg <- cv.tree(tree.fit)
best.size <- cv.reg$size[which.min(cv.reg$dev)]

plot(cv.reg$size, cv.reg$dev, type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "Number of terminal nodes", ylab = "CV deviance",
     main = "Choosing the tree size by cross-validation")
points(best.size, min(cv.reg$dev), col = "darkorange", pch = 19, cex = 2)
cat("Tree size with the lowest CV deviance:", best.size, "\n")
```

```{r}
pruned.tree <- prune.tree(tree.fit, best = best.size)

pred_tree   <- predict(tree.fit,    newdata = test_tree)
pred_pruned <- predict(pruned.tree, newdata = test_tree)
m_tree   <- test_metrics(pred_tree,   test_tree$rel_log_cost_m2)
m_pruned <- test_metrics(pred_pruned, test_tree$rel_log_cost_m2)

results <- add_result(results, "Regression tree (full)",   "drivers + region", metrics = m_tree)
results <- add_result(results, paste0("Regression tree (pruned, ", best.size, " leaves)"),
                      "drivers + region", metrics = m_pruned)
paste("Test MSE: full tree", round(m_tree[["test_MSE"]], 5),
      " pruned tree", round(m_pruned[["test_MSE"]], 5))
```

If the CV curve chose the full tree, pruning changes nothing and the two rows
are identical — that happens when `tree()`'s default stopping rule already
grew a modest tree. A single tree is easy to read and usually the weakest
predictor in this section; it is here for the picture, and as the building
block of the next two models.

## Bagging and random forest

Bagging grows many trees on bootstrap samples of the training rows and
averages them; a random forest does the same but offers each split only a
random subset of the drivers, which de-correlates the trees. In
`randomForest()` the only difference is `mtry`: all predictors for bagging,
about a third of them for a regression forest.

```{r}
num_predictors <- ncol(train_tree) - 1     # 11 drivers + region

set.seed(462)
bag.tree <- randomForest(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = train_tree,
                         mtry = num_predictors, ntree = 500, importance = TRUE)
set.seed(462)
rf.tree  <- randomForest(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = train_tree,
                         mtry = 4, ntree = 500, importance = TRUE)
bag.tree
rf.tree
```

The printed "% Var explained" is out-of-bag — each row predicted only by the
trees that did not see it — so it is an honest training-side estimate without
a validation set.

```{r, fig.height = 5, out.width = '100%'}
varImpPlot(rf.tree, main = "Random forest: variable importance", cex = 0.8)
```

```{r}
importance(rf.tree) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("driver") %>%
  arrange(desc(`%IncMSE`)) %>%
  mutate(across(-driver, ~ round(.x, 2))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Random forest importance: % increase in MSE when the driver is permuted, and node purity")
```

`%IncMSE` is the one to read: how much worse the out-of-bag predictions get
when that driver's values are shuffled. It is model-agnostic in spirit and the
closest thing a forest has to the standardised coefficients of section 4, so
the two rankings can be compared directly — a driver that is near the top in
both the lasso table and here is important in any reasonable model.

```{r}
pred_bag <- predict(bag.tree, newdata = test_tree)
pred_rf  <- predict(rf.tree,  newdata = test_tree)
m_bag <- test_metrics(pred_bag, test_tree$rel_log_cost_m2)
m_rf  <- test_metrics(pred_rf,  test_tree$rel_log_cost_m2)

results <- add_result(results, "Bagging (mtry = 12)",       "drivers + region", metrics = m_bag)
results <- add_result(results, "Random forest (mtry = 4)",  "drivers + region", metrics = m_rf)
paste("Test MSE: bagging", round(m_bag[["test_MSE"]], 5), " random forest", round(m_rf[["test_MSE"]], 5))
```

## Boosting

Boosting grows small trees one after another, each fitted to the residuals of
the ensemble so far, scaled down by the shrinkage. For a continuous response
the distribution is `"gaussian"`. Module 6 uses stumps (`interaction.depth =
1`); depth 2 lets each tree hold one interaction, which section 3 suggested
exists.

```{r}
set.seed(462)
boost.fit <- gbm(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = train_tree,
                 distribution = "gaussian", n.trees = 1000,
                 interaction.depth = 2, shrinkage = 0.05, verbose = FALSE)

# relative influence: share of the total reduction in squared error attributed to each driver
summary(boost.fit, plotit = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(rel.inf = round(rel.inf, 2)) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Boosting: relative influence of each driver")
```

```{r}
pred_boost <- predict(boost.fit, newdata = test_tree, n.trees = 1000, type = "response")
m_boost <- test_metrics(pred_boost, test_tree$rel_log_cost_m2)
results <- add_result(results, "Boosting (1000 trees, depth 2)", "drivers + region", metrics = m_boost)
paste("The test MSE of the boosted model is", round(m_boost[["test_MSE"]], 5))
```

Three importance rankings now exist — lasso coefficients, forest `%IncMSE`,
boosting relative influence. Section 6 puts them side by side.

## Tuning the ensembles and the elastic net

The forest and the boosted model above use settings chosen by habit —
`mtry = 4` and `nodesize = 5`; 1,000 trees at depth 2 with shrinkage 0.05 —
and the ridge and lasso are the two endpoints of the elastic net. This
section asks whether any of those choices matter, using the same five
time-block folds as section 4.2 so that every setting is judged on years it
did not see. The test set is not touched until one setting per model has been
chosen.

```{r}
# blocked cross-validation: fit on four year-blocks, score on the fifth, repeat
cv_blocked <- function(fit_fun, pred_fun, data, foldid) {
  sapply(sort(unique(foldid)), function(k) {
    fit  <- fit_fun(data[foldid != k, ])
    pred <- pred_fun(fit, data[foldid == k, ])
    sqrt(mean((data$rel_log_cost_m2[foldid == k] - pred)^2))
  })
}
```

### Random forest: `mtry` and `nodesize`

`nodesize` is the smallest leaf the forest is allowed to grow; small leaves
memorise individual district-quarters, large ones average over them. `mtry`
is how many drivers each split may choose from. Six combinations, 300 trees
each inside the folds (enough to rank settings; the chosen one is refitted
with 500).

```{r tune-rf, cache = TRUE}
rf_grid <- expand.grid(mtry = c(4, 12), nodesize = c(5, 20, 50))

rf_cv <- map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(rf_grid)), function(i) {
  set.seed(462)
  fold_rmse <- cv_blocked(
    fit_fun  = function(d) randomForest(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = d, ntree = 300,
                                        mtry = rf_grid$mtry[i], nodesize = rf_grid$nodesize[i]),
    pred_fun = function(fit, d) predict(fit, newdata = d),
    data = train_tree, foldid = foldid)
  tibble(mtry = rf_grid$mtry[i], nodesize = rf_grid$nodesize[i],
         cv_RMSE = mean(fold_rmse), cv_RMSE_se = sd(fold_rmse) / sqrt(length(fold_rmse)))
})

rf_cv %>%
  arrange(cv_RMSE) %>%
  mutate(across(c(cv_RMSE, cv_RMSE_se), ~ round(.x, 5))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Random forest: blocked-CV RMSE by mtry and nodesize")

rf_best <- rf_cv %>% arrange(cv_RMSE) %>% slice(1)
cat("Chosen: mtry =", rf_best$mtry, " nodesize =", rf_best$nodesize, "\n")
```

```{r}
set.seed(462)
rf_tuned.tree <- randomForest(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = train_tree, ntree = 500,
                              mtry = rf_best$mtry, nodesize = rf_best$nodesize, importance = TRUE)

m_rf_tuned <- test_metrics(predict(rf_tuned.tree, newdata = test_tree), test_tree$rel_log_cost_m2)
results <- add_result(results, paste0("Random forest (tuned: mtry = ", rf_best$mtry,
                                      ", nodesize = ", rf_best$nodesize, ")"),
                      "drivers + region", metrics = m_rf_tuned)
paste("Test MSE: untuned forest", round(m_rf[["test_MSE"]], 5),
      " tuned forest", round(m_rf_tuned[["test_MSE"]], 5))
```

The forest is insensitive to both settings: the six combinations span
0.0862–0.0871 in CV RMSE with a standard error of about 0.003 on each, so
nothing separates them, and the habit choice (`mtry = 4`, `nodesize = 5`)
happens to sit at the top. The tuned and untuned test errors are therefore
identical (0.01140). The worry that 5-row leaves were memorising
district-quarters does not show up — averaging 500 trees already smooths
that away — and the forest's answer is settled by the drivers it is given,
not by how it is grown.

### Boosting: shrinkage, depth and the number of trees

Boosting's settings interact: a smaller shrinkage needs more trees, and a
deeper tree needs fewer. Four combinations of shrinkage and depth; for each,
the number of trees is chosen on the folds by scoring the ensemble every 100
trees (one `predict()` call per fold returns all of them at once).

```{r tune-gbm, cache = TRUE}
gbm_grid  <- expand.grid(shrinkage = c(0.01, 0.05), depth = c(2, 4))
tree_seq  <- seq(100, 3000, by = 100)

gbm_cv <- map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(gbm_grid)), function(i) {
  # per fold: RMSE at every candidate number of trees
  fold_curves <- sapply(sort(unique(foldid)), function(k) {
    set.seed(462)
    fit <- gbm(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = train_tree[foldid != k, ],
               distribution = "gaussian", n.trees = max(tree_seq),
               interaction.depth = gbm_grid$depth[i], shrinkage = gbm_grid$shrinkage[i],
               verbose = FALSE)
    preds <- predict(fit, newdata = train_tree[foldid == k, ], n.trees = tree_seq, type = "response")
    sqrt(colMeans((train_tree$rel_log_cost_m2[foldid == k] - preds)^2))
  })
  curve <- rowMeans(fold_curves)                       # mean RMSE across folds at each n.trees
  tibble(shrinkage = gbm_grid$shrinkage[i], depth = gbm_grid$depth[i],
         n_trees = tree_seq[which.min(curve)], cv_RMSE = min(curve),
         cv_RMSE_se = sd(fold_curves[which.min(curve), ]) / sqrt(ncol(fold_curves)),
         curve = list(tibble(n_trees = tree_seq, cv_RMSE = curve)))
})

gbm_cv %>%
  dplyr::select(-curve) %>%
  arrange(cv_RMSE) %>%
  mutate(across(c(cv_RMSE, cv_RMSE_se), ~ round(.x, 5))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Boosting: blocked-CV RMSE at the best number of trees for each shrinkage x depth")

gbm_best <- gbm_cv %>% arrange(cv_RMSE) %>% slice(1)
cat("Chosen: shrinkage =", gbm_best$shrinkage, " depth =", gbm_best$depth,
    " n.trees =", gbm_best$n_trees, "\n")
```

```{r}
gbm_cv %>%
  dplyr::select(shrinkage, depth, curve) %>%
  unnest(curve) %>%
  mutate(setting = paste0("shrinkage ", shrinkage, ", depth ", depth)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n_trees, y = cv_RMSE, colour = setting)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Boosting: blocked-CV RMSE against the number of trees",
       x = "Number of trees", y = "Mean CV RMSE across the five blocks", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
set.seed(462)
boost_tuned.fit <- gbm(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = train_tree,
                       distribution = "gaussian", n.trees = gbm_best$n_trees,
                       interaction.depth = gbm_best$depth, shrinkage = gbm_best$shrinkage,
                       verbose = FALSE)

m_boost_tuned <- test_metrics(predict(boost_tuned.fit, newdata = test_tree,
                                      n.trees = gbm_best$n_trees, type = "response"),
                              test_tree$rel_log_cost_m2)
results <- add_result(results, paste0("Boosting (tuned: ", gbm_best$n_trees, " trees, depth ",
                                      gbm_best$depth, ", shrinkage ", gbm_best$shrinkage, ")"),
                      "drivers + region", metrics = m_boost_tuned)
paste("Test MSE: untuned boosting", round(m_boost[["test_MSE"]], 5),
      " tuned boosting", round(m_boost_tuned[["test_MSE"]], 5))
```

This is the one tuning that paid. Depth matters more than shrinkage: both
depth-4 settings reach a CV RMSE of 0.0880, both depth-2 settings stop at
0.089–0.090, a gap of about one standard error but consistent across the
folds. Shrinkage 0.05 at depth 4 bottoms out at 1,100 trees and then climbs
— past that point it is fitting noise — while shrinkage 0.01 at depth 4 is
still edging down at 3,000 trees and would probably match or just pass it
with a longer grid, for a gain in the fourth decimal. The chosen setting
(0.05, depth 4, 1,100 trees) tests at 0.01138, against 0.01224 for the
habit setting, which moves boosting from fourth place to level with the
forests. The reason depth helps fits what the single tree showed: the useful
structure is region-by-driver, which a depth-2 tree can only half express.

### Elastic net: `alpha` between ridge and lasso

`alpha` mixes the two penalties — 0 is ridge, 1 is lasso. Five values, each
tuned for $\lambda$ on the same folds, compared at `lambda.min` (section 4.5
showed the one-SE rule is too blunt on these folds).

```{r}
alpha_grid <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)

enet_cv <- map_dfr(alpha_grid, function(a) {
  fit <- cv.glmnet(x_train_reg, y_train, alpha = a, foldid = foldid)
  tibble(alpha = a,
         lambda_min = fit$lambda.min,
         cv_RMSE = sqrt(min(fit$cvm)),
         n_nonzero = sum(as.vector(coef(fit, s = "lambda.min"))[-1] != 0),
         fit = list(fit))
})

enet_cv %>%
  dplyr::select(-fit) %>%
  mutate(across(c(lambda_min, cv_RMSE), ~ round(.x, 5))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Elastic net (drivers + region): blocked-CV RMSE at lambda.min by alpha")

enet_best <- enet_cv %>% arrange(cv_RMSE) %>% slice(1)
m_enet <- test_metrics(as.vector(predict(enet_best$fit[[1]], newx = x_test_reg, s = "lambda.min")), y_test)
results <- add_result(results, paste0("Elastic net (alpha = ", enet_best$alpha, ", lambda.min)"),
                      "drivers + region", metrics = m_enet)
cat("Chosen alpha:", enet_best$alpha, " test MSE:", round(m_enet[["test_MSE"]], 5), "\n")
```

A flat line, as expected: CV RMSE runs from 0.0961 at `alpha = 0` to 0.0958
at `alpha = 1`, a spread of 0.0003 with all five mixtures keeping 19–27 of
the 27 columns. The lasso wins by a hair and tests identically to its
section 4.6 row (0.01356). On this data the choice of penalty is cosmetic
and the choice of features is not, which is the sentence for the poster.

::: {.boxNote}
**Why the relative response matters most for the trees.** Every tree model
here predicts a leaf mean learnt from 1996–2019 rows. Asked about 2024, a
forest fitted on log *real* $/m² can only return costs it saw before 2020,
and under-predicts every test year by the whole post-2019 rise. On the
relative response there is no trend to miss: a district 20% dearer than the
rest of the country in 2019 is predicted 20% dearer in 2024, which is the
right kind of guess. Section 6.7 shows the size of the gap on the real
response.
:::

*A dozen models, one test set. Which is best, and does the answer depend on
the model?*

# Evaluate performance

## Sensitivity: the two early-years drivers

The headline frame starts in 1996 because `dwell_per_1000` and `houses_yoy`
do not exist before then. One row to show what that cost: the multiple linear
regression without those two drivers, fitted on all 7,051 training rows from
1990Q2 and tested on all 1,611 test rows.

```{r}
drivers_9 <- setdiff(drivers, c("dwell_per_1000", "houses_yoy"))

train_9 <- df_train %>% dplyr::select(rel_log_cost_m2, all_of(drivers_9))
test_9  <- df_test  %>% dplyr::select(rel_log_cost_m2, all_of(drivers_9))
mlr_9.fit <- lm(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = train_9)

# same drivers on the headline frame, so the only difference is the rows
mlr_9c.fit <- lm(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = train_drv %>% dplyr::select(rel_log_cost_m2, all_of(drivers_9)))

m_9  <- test_metrics(predict(mlr_9.fit,  test_9),  test_9$rel_log_cost_m2)
m_9c <- test_metrics(predict(mlr_9c.fit, test_drv), test_drv$rel_log_cost_m2)

results <- add_result(results, "MLR, 9 drivers, all rows 1990+", "sensitivity",
                      summary(mlr_9.fit)$r.squared, summary(mlr_9.fit)$adj.r.squared, m_9)
results <- add_result(results, "MLR, 9 drivers, headline rows",  "sensitivity",
                      summary(mlr_9c.fit)$r.squared, summary(mlr_9c.fit)$adj.r.squared, m_9c)

cat(sprintf("Rows: %d (1990+) vs %d (1996+)\n", nrow(train_9), nrow(train_drv)))
cat(sprintf("Test MSE, 9 drivers: %.5f on 1990+ rows, %.5f on 1996+ rows; 11 drivers on 1996+: %.5f\n",
            m_9[["test_MSE"]], m_9c[["test_MSE"]], m_mlr[["test_MSE"]]))
```

Two comparisons fall out. The second row against the first says what the
1990–95 rows add when the drivers are held fixed; the second row against the
headline MLR says what the two dropped drivers add when the rows are held
fixed. If the second gap is the larger, keeping the drivers was the right
trade.

## Goodness-of-fit (training data)

$$R^2 = \frac{TSS - RSS}{TSS}, \qquad
  \bar R^2 = 1 - \frac{RSS / (n - p - 1)}{TSS / (n - 1)}$$

```{r}
results %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(train_R2)) %>%
  dplyr::select(model, set, train_R2, adj_R2) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Training R2 and adjusted R2 for the least-squares models")

cat("For reference, the out-of-bag % variance explained: bagging",
    round(tail(bag.tree$rsq, 1) * 100, 1), " random forest", round(tail(rf.tree$rsq, 1) * 100, 1), "\n")
```

The district-fixed-effects model is the ceiling: no model of measured drivers
should be expected to beat it on the training data, and the distance between
it and the best drivers-only model is the share of the between-district
difference that the drivers do not explain.

## Test MSE and RMSE (2020Q1–2026Q2)

```{r}
results_test <- results %>%
  arrange(test_RMSE) %>%
  mutate(rank = row_number()) %>%
  dplyr::select(rank, model, set, test_MSE, test_RMSE, test_R2)

results_test %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 5))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Every model on the same 1,611 test district-quarters, best first")
```

```{r, fig.height = 6}
results_test %>%
  mutate(model = fct_reorder(paste(model, "-", set), -test_RMSE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = model, y = test_RMSE, fill = set)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = sqrt(mean((y_test - y_train_mean)^2)), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Test RMSE by model (dashed line: predict the training mean)",
       x = NULL, y = "Test RMSE (log relative cost)", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

A test RMSE of 0.10 on a log scale means a typical prediction is about 10%
off the district's actual cost relative to the rest of New Zealand. The
dashed line is the no-model baseline. Read the table with two questions:
which model is best, and how far apart are the models — if the spread among
the sensible models is a few thousandths of RMSE, the choice of model matters
much less than the choice of drivers, and the poster should say so.

## Comparison with Niwesh's build

Niwesh's `03_rq1_models.Rmd` fitted the same response on the same quarters
(his frame is ours minus Chatham Islands and Kawerau, two training rows) with
different packages (`glmnet` with his own tuning loop, `ranger`, `rpart`).
His test results are in `t09_test_results.csv`; where the two builds share a
model, the test RMSE should agree to the third decimal. Where they do not,
the reason is a difference in method and should be nameable.

```{r}
niwesh_file <- file.path(data_root, "t09_test_results.csv")

if (file.exists(niwesh_file)) {
  niwesh <- read_csv(niwesh_file, show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
    dplyr::select(niwesh_model = model, niwesh_set = set, niwesh_test_RMSE = test_rmse, niwesh_test_R2 = test_r2)

  # the pairs of models that are the same thing in both builds
  model_pairs <- tribble(
    ~model,                               ~set,                 ~niwesh_model,       ~niwesh_set,
    "Multiple linear regression",         "drivers",            "Linear regression", "drivers",
    "Multiple linear regression",         "drivers + district", "Linear regression", "district",
    "Ridge (lambda.1se)",                 "drivers",            "Ridge",             "drivers",
    "Lasso (lambda.1se)",                 "drivers",            "Lasso",             "drivers",
    "Random forest (mtry = 4)",           "drivers + region",   "Random forest",     "drivers")

  comparison <- model_pairs %>%
    inner_join(results, by = c("model", "set")) %>%
    inner_join(niwesh, by = c("niwesh_model", "niwesh_set")) %>%
    mutate(diff_RMSE = test_RMSE - niwesh_test_RMSE) %>%
    dplyr::select(model, set, test_RMSE, niwesh_model, niwesh_set, niwesh_test_RMSE, diff_RMSE, test_R2, niwesh_test_R2)

  comparison %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4))) %>%
    knitr::kable(caption = "Our test RMSE vs Niwesh's for the models both builds fitted")
} else {
  cat("t09_test_results.csv not found in", data_root, "- comparison skipped.\n")
}
```

The two linear regressions are the same estimator on the same drivers, so
their gap (0.0045 RMSE on the drivers set, 0.0020 with district) is larger
than it should be. Two rows differ in training, but three differ in the test
set — Chatham Islands and Kawerau have one and two test rows — and a tiny
district can carry a very large error. Our MLR scored on exactly his 1,608
test rows:

```{r}
his_test_rows <- !df_test_c$ta %in% c("Chatham Islands Territory", "Kawerau District")

cat(sprintf("MLR, drivers:            RMSE %.4f on all %d test rows, %.4f on Niwesh's %d\n",
            sqrt(mean((test_drv$rel_log_cost_m2 - pred_mlr)^2)), nrow(test_drv),
            sqrt(mean((test_drv$rel_log_cost_m2[his_test_rows] - pred_mlr[his_test_rows])^2)), sum(his_test_rows)))
cat(sprintf("MLR, drivers + district: RMSE %.4f on all %d test rows, %.4f on Niwesh's %d\n",
            sqrt(mean((test_ta$rel_log_cost_m2 - pred_mlr_ta)^2)), nrow(test_ta),
            sqrt(mean((test_ta$rel_log_cost_m2[his_test_rows] - pred_mlr_ta[his_test_rows])^2)), sum(his_test_rows)))

# the three rows themselves
df_test_c %>%
  dplyr::filter(!his_test_rows) %>%
  mutate(predicted = pred_mlr[!his_test_rows], error = rel_log_cost_m2 - predicted) %>%
  dplyr::select(ta, yq, houses_n, rel_log_cost_m2, predicted, error) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "The three test rows Niwesh's build does not score")
```

The gap does not close. On his 1,608 rows our drivers-only regression
scores 0.1202 against his 0.1162, and the district regression 0.1084
against his 0.1066: the Chatham Islands row (five houses, error 0.49) was
worth 0.0006 and the rest remains. Same estimator, same eleven drivers by
name, same response, same quarters — so the difference is upstream, in what
each build fed the model. Candidates, in the order I would check them on
Monday: whether his `drivers` set is the same eleven columns (his VIF table
lists them, but a feature set for fitting can differ from one for a VIF
check); whether he standardised or transformed any driver before `lm()`;
whether his train rows are the 5,694 the README says or a different cut.
Until this is understood neither number goes on the poster. The
other pairings differ for known reasons. Ridge and lasso: his tuning chose
$\lambda \approx 0.0004$, which is OLS in all but name, while our
`lambda.1se` values are 300–3,000 times larger — compare his numbers with our
`lambda.min` rows instead, which sit within 0.001 of OLS. Random forest: ours
has `region` and his does not, and it is 0.0066 RMSE better for it — the same
lesson as section 4.6, that geography is worth more than any tuning.

## Which drivers matter — three rankings side by side

```{r}
rank_lasso <- coef_table %>%
  transmute(driver, lasso = abs(`Lasso (1se)`)) %>%
  mutate(lasso_rank = min_rank(-lasso))

rank_rf <- importance(rf.tree) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("driver") %>%
  transmute(driver, rf = `%IncMSE`) %>%
  mutate(rf_rank = min_rank(-rf))

rank_boost <- summary(boost.fit, plotit = FALSE) %>%
  transmute(driver = as.character(var), boost = rel.inf) %>%
  mutate(boost_rank = min_rank(-boost))

rank_lasso %>%
  full_join(rank_rf, by = "driver") %>%
  full_join(rank_boost, by = "driver") %>%
  dplyr::filter(driver %in% drivers) %>%
  mutate(mean_rank = rowMeans(cbind(lasso_rank, rf_rank, boost_rank), na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  arrange(mean_rank) %>%
  mutate(across(c(lasso, rf, boost, mean_rank), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Driver rankings: lasso |coefficient| (1se), forest %IncMSE, boosting relative influence")
```

This is the table that answers the "which parameters are important" half of
RQ1. A driver ranked near the top by all three — a linear model with
selection, a bagged ensemble with permutation importance, and a boosted
ensemble — is important in a way that does not depend on the modelling
choice. A driver that is high in one and low in the others is picking up
something model-specific (the forest and boosting can use a driver through
interactions that the lasso cannot see), and the text should say which.

## Bootstrap standard errors for the headline coefficients

Module 5's check on the standard errors `summary()` reports: refit the
drivers-only linear model on 100 bootstrap samples of the training rows and
take the standard deviation of each coefficient across refits. If the
bootstrap SE is much larger than the formula SE, the formula's assumptions
(independent, equal-variance errors) are being strained — plausible here,
since the 5,696 rows are 67 districts observed repeatedly.

```{r}
set.seed(462)
bootstrap_samples <- replicate(n = 100,
                               expr = train_drv[sample(1:nrow(train_drv), replace = TRUE), ],
                               simplify = FALSE)

boot_fits  <- lapply(bootstrap_samples, function(s) lm(rel_log_cost_m2 ~ ., data = s))
boot_coefs <- sapply(boot_fits, coef)      # one column per bootstrap fit

# the three drivers with the largest standardised OLS coefficients
top3 <- std_coef(mlr.fit, train_drv) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(std_coefficient))) %>%
  slice(1:3) %>% pull(driver)

tibble(driver = top3,
       estimate     = coef(mlr.fit)[top3],
       formula_SE   = summary(mlr.fit)$coefficients[top3, "Std. Error"],
       bootstrap_SE = apply(boot_coefs[top3, , drop = FALSE], 1, sd),
       boot_CI_low  = apply(boot_coefs[top3, , drop = FALSE], 1, quantile, probs = 0.025),
       boot_CI_high = apply(boot_coefs[top3, , drop = FALSE], 1, quantile, probs = 0.975)) %>%
  mutate(ratio = bootstrap_SE / formula_SE,
         across(-driver, ~ round(.x, 4))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Formula vs bootstrap standard errors, 100 bootstrap refits")

confint(mlr.fit)[top3, ]
```

```{r}
ggplot(data.frame(b = boot_coefs[top3[1], ]), aes(x = b)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = coef(mlr.fit)[top3[1]], colour = "darkorange", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = paste("Bootstrap distribution of the coefficient on", top3[1]),
       x = "Coefficient across 100 bootstrap refits", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

A ratio near 1 says the formula SEs can be trusted; a ratio well above 1 says
the real uncertainty is larger and the confidence intervals in section 3
should be read as optimistic. Note what the bootstrap does *not* fix: rows
from the same district are resampled independently, so district-level
clustering is still ignored. A block bootstrap by district would be the
stricter check, and is outside this document's scope.

## The real response and the extrapolation problem

Finally, the response as the pitch worded it: log real $/m² itself. Two
models, the ones at the two extremes of the extrapolation question — the
drivers-plus-district linear model, which carries a straight-line trend in
`t_index`, and the random forest, which cannot extrapolate at all.

```{r}
train_real    <- df_train_c %>% dplyr::select(log_real_cost_m2, all_of(drivers), ta)
test_real     <- df_test_c  %>% dplyr::select(log_real_cost_m2, all_of(drivers), ta)
train_real_rf <- as.data.frame(df_train_c %>% dplyr::select(log_real_cost_m2, all_of(drivers), region))
test_real_rf  <- as.data.frame(df_test_c  %>% dplyr::select(log_real_cost_m2, all_of(drivers), region))

mlr_real.fit <- lm(log_real_cost_m2 ~ ., data = train_real)
set.seed(462)
rf_real.tree <- randomForest(log_real_cost_m2 ~ ., data = train_real_rf, mtry = 4, ntree = 500)

pred_real_lm <- predict(mlr_real.fit, newdata = test_real)
pred_real_rf <- predict(rf_real.tree, newdata = test_real_rf)

real_metrics <- function(pred, actual) {
  c(test_RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - pred)^2)),
    test_R2   = 1 - sum((actual - pred)^2) / sum((actual - mean(train_real$log_real_cost_m2))^2),
    mean_bias = mean(pred - actual))
}

rbind(`MLR, drivers + district` = real_metrics(pred_real_lm, test_real$log_real_cost_m2),
      `Random forest, drivers + region` = real_metrics(pred_real_rf, test_real$log_real_cost_m2)) %>%
  round(4) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Log real $/m2 as the response: test RMSE, R2 and mean bias (negative = under-prediction)")
```

```{r}
df_test_c %>%
  mutate(`MLR + district` = pred_real_lm, `Random forest` = pred_real_rf) %>%
  dplyr::select(year, actual = log_real_cost_m2, `MLR + district`, `Random forest`) %>%
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "series", values_to = "value") %>%
  group_by(year, series) %>%
  summarise(mean_real = mean(exp(value)), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_real, colour = series)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Real $/m2 in the test years: actual vs predicted (mean over districts)",
       x = "Year", y = "Real $/m2, June-2026 dollars", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Two things in this figure are easy to misread. First, in June-2026 dollars
the test years are nearly flat — the national mean sits between about $3,180
and $3,340 per m² across 2020–2026, dipping in 2022 and rising through 2024.
The 2021–23 cost spike that everyone remembers is a *nominal* spike, and the
CGPI deflator has taken most of it out; what is left is the few percent by
which house prices outran the construction price index. Second, the $R^2$
values (0.75 and 0.70) are far higher than anything in the relative-cost
tables, not because the models are better but because the between-district
differences are back in the response and both models carry location.

Within that, the extrapolation problem shows as predicted, at a smaller
scale: the forest sits about 4% low across the whole test period (mean bias
−0.042) and drifts lower after 2022, because its `t_index` leaves end at 2019
and nothing in the drivers tells it that real costs kept rising; the linear
model's straight trend tracks the level well (bias +0.011) but overshoots by
2026. Neither is a safe way to forecast real dollars. The relative model is
the one to trust across districts, and real $/m² is best answered as "the
national series times the district's relative position", which is how the
poster should put it.

## Where this leaves RQ1

The three parts of the answer, each pointing at the table or figure that
supports it:

Location first. Adding the district to the linear model lifts adjusted $R^2$
from 0.19 to 0.40 (section 3.4), and the same districts sit at the top and
bottom of the ranking for thirty years (section 2.2) — Queenstown-Lakes 16%
above the rest of the country at the median, Wellington City 11%, Ōpōtiki 17%
below. Whatever makes them so is mostly not in this dataset — land,
remoteness, the kind of houses being built. The three regional dummies the
lasso keeps (section 4.6: Wellington and Hawke's Bay dear, Manawatū-Whanganui
cheap) are the compact list of where that unexplained premium sits after the
drivers have had their say.

Of the drivers we can measure, two survive every model: residential
alteration spending and new dwellings per 1,000 residents. They are the first
two forward selection picks (section 3.5), the only two the lasso keeps at
`lambda.1se` (section 4.4), and the top two in both the forest's permutation
importance and boosting's relative influence once `region` is set aside
(section 6.5). The number of houses consented is a clear third in the linear
models and the time index third in the tree models; the rest add little. The
within-district coefficients (section 3.4) give the sizes — about +0.03 in
log relative cost per SD of alteration spending, +0.004 per SD of population
pressure once district is held fixed — and the bootstrap (section 6.6) says
the formula standard errors understate the uncertainty by only 8–13%.

The models fall into two bands, and the band matters more than the model.
Anything that carries geography — bagging, tuned boosting and the random
forest (test RMSE 0.106–0.107), the district-effects regression (0.109),
even untuned boosting (0.111) — beats anything that has only the eleven
drivers (0.121–0.129), and within a band the choice of algorithm moves the
error by a few thousandths. Section 5.4 makes the same point from the other
side: a tuning grid over the forest changed nothing, over the elastic net
changed nothing, and over boosting moved it from the bottom of the upper
band to the top of it. The poster
should lead with that: location explains most of the difference between
districts, two measured drivers explain a useful part of the rest, and the
algorithm is the least important choice. Niwesh's independent build (section
6.4) landing in the same places — his district regression at 0.107, his
forest at 0.113 without region — is the check that this is a property of the
data and not of one person's code; the one open gap, 0.004 on the
drivers-only regression after scoring on his rows, is Monday's first
question.

*End of document (stages 1–6; section 7, extensions, to follow)*
